dna: Western art music tradition spanning 600+ years, from medieval chant to contemporary concert halls. Complex time signatures, rubato, and tempo ranges from adagio (60 BPM) to presto (180+ BPM).
Sonata form (exposition–development–recapitulation), rondo (ABACA), theme and variations, fugue with subject and countersubject, and concerto form with solo-orchestral dialogue.
Strings (violin, viola, cello, double bass), woodwinds (flute, oboe, clarinet, bassoon), brass (French horn, trumpet, trombone), piano, harpsichord, and timpani.

Functional tonal harmony built on counterpoint and voice leading. Rich modulations between keys, diminished seventh chords, Neapolitan sixths, augmented sixths (Italian, French, German), and cadential patterns.

sub.d: Ornamental counterpoint, basso continuo, terraced dynamics, and concerto grosso forms from Bach and Vivaldi.
Emotionally expressive, expanded orchestras, virtuosic solos, and dramatic dynamic contrasts from Chopin to Mahler.
Lush tone colors, whole-tone and pentatonic scales, blurred rhythms, and atmospheric textures from Debussy and Ravel.
Repetitive patterns, gradual phasing, consonant harmony, and hypnotic pulse from Reich, Glass, and Riley.
Extended techniques, atonality, electronic integration, and experimental timbres pushing the boundaries of tradition.
Orchestral storytelling for cinema — leitmotifs, sweeping themes, and dramatic underscoring from Williams to Zimmer.

dna: Rooted in the film scoring tradition of Hollywood's Golden Age, shaped by pioneers like Max Steiner, Bernard Herrmann, John Williams, and Hans Zimmer. Modern cinematic music blends orchestral tradition with electronic production, creating hybrid scores that span intimate underscore to massive trailer anthems.

Built around thematic development and leitmotifs — recurring musical themes tied to characters, places, or ideas. Dramatic arcs mirror on-screen action: tension builds through rising dynamics, rhythmic acceleration, and harmonic tension, releasing into resolution or cliffhanger moments.

Full symphony orchestra at the core — strings for emotion, brass for power, woodwinds for color. Augmented by choir (SATB and wordless), hybrid synthesizers, processed percussion, taiko drums, trailer impacts (risers, hits, booms), piano, and solo instruments (cello, violin, French horn) for intimate moments.

Layered textures create depth and width — from intimate solo instruments to massive tutti sections. Wide stereo imaging, extreme dynamic range (from pppp to ffff), and cinematic production techniques like sub-bass drops, reverse swells, granular synthesis, and trailer-style sound design define the modern cinematic palette.

sub.d: Grand, powerful compositions with full orchestra, choir, and percussion. Used for blockbuster trailers, action sequences, and heroic moments. Think Two Steps from Hell and Audiomachine.
Purpose-built for movie trailers with structured builds, impacts, and emotional peaks. Features hybrid production combining orchestral power with electronic sound design and massive percussion.
Subtle background music that supports dialogue and scene emotion without competing for attention. Gentle textures, ambient pads, sparse instrumentation, and careful dynamic control.
Fuses orchestral elements with electronic production — synthesizers, processed beats, and sound design layered with traditional instruments. Pioneered by Hans Zimmer's modern approach and Junkie XL.
Evocative music for non-fiction storytelling. Often features world instruments, ambient textures, and emotionally resonant themes that enhance real-world narratives without melodrama.

Tension-building music using dissonance, extended techniques, and unsettling textures. Cluster chords, prepared piano, bowed metal, and sudden stingers create fear and unease. Defined by composers like Penderecki and Mansell.

dna: Phonk traces directly to 1990s Memphis rap — Three 6 Mafia, DJ Spanish Fly, and Tommy Wright III pioneered the dark, lo-fi sound. Modern phonk emerged around 2015 when producers like DJ Smokey and Soudiere began chopping and flipping Memphis vocals over heavy trap-influenced beats. The genre exploded on TikTok and YouTube through drift car edits and gym culture.

Phonk tracks are loop-based and hypnotic — a 4–8 bar pattern repeats with subtle variations and sample drops. Structure is minimal: intro, main loop, variations with added or removed elements, and outro. No traditional verse-chorus form. The repetition is intentional, creating a trance-like, aggressive groove designed for driving and workout montages.

The cowbell is phonk's most recognizable element — a driving rhythmic pattern that defines the genre. Distorted and clipped 808 bass provides the low-end weight. Chopped and screwed vocal samples from 1990s Memphis rap are pitched down, drenched in reverb, and scattered across the beat. Dark synth pads and eerie melodies add atmosphere.

Heavy saturation and distortion on the 808 bass create that characteristic rattling, clipped sound. Sidechaining the kick to the bass produces a pumping effect. Lo-fi processing — vinyl crackle, tape hiss, bit reduction — gives tracks an aged, underground feel. Reverb and delay on vocal chops create depth and space in an otherwise aggressive mix.

sub.d: The viral subgenre — aggressive cowbell patterns, distorted 808s, and dark energy designed to soundtrack car drift edits. Kordhell and DVRST brought it mainstream.
Closer to the original Memphis rap roots — heavy vocal chops from Three 6 Mafia-era samples, lo-fi drums, and dark atmospheric production.
Phonk infused with Brazilian funk rhythms — faster tempos, MC vocal chants, heavy bass, and a high-energy party atmosphere. Huge in Brazilian car culture.
Phonk's dark aesthetic applied to four-on-the-floor house rhythms. Punchy kicks, filtered cowbells, and distorted bass grooves designed for club play.
Slower and more atmospheric — lo-fi textures, spacious reverb, melodic samples, and a laid-back groove. Playamane and fkbambam favor the relaxed side.
Maximum aggression for workout motivation — louder, faster, harder. Heavy distortion, rapid cowbell patterns, and intense 808 drops timed for heavy lifts.

Sparse but punchy — minimal elements with maximum groove. Clean mixes prioritize vocals and percussion. Heavy use of reverb on guitars and delay on vocal ad-libs.

dna: Amapiano ('the pianos') emerged in South Africa's Gauteng province around 2012, fusing deep house, jazz, and kwaito. Pioneered by producers like Kabza De Small, DJ Maphorisa, and Vigro Deep, it grew from township parties to dominate South African music by 2019. By 2022, it had become a global phenomenon, influencing pop, Afrobeats, and dance music worldwide through artists like Uncle Waffles and Major League DJz.

Amapiano tracks are groove-driven and evolve through layering rather than traditional verse-chorus structures. A typical arrangement builds from a minimal percussion loop, gradually adding log drums, bass, keys, and vocal elements. Breakdowns strip back to core percussion before rebuilding. Tracks often feature extended instrumental sections for DJ mixing, with vocal hooks appearing as textural elements rather than structural anchors.

The log drum is Amapiano's most distinctive element — a tuned percussion sound that carries the melodic rhythm. Deep, warm sub-bass provides the foundation. Rhodes or Wurlitzer electric piano adds jazzy chord voicings. Shakers, congas, and organic percussion create polyrhythmic layers. Vocal samples — often pitched, chopped, or looped — add human texture without dominating the mix.

Amapiano production prioritizes groove and space. Every element serves the rhythm — even harmonic instruments play percussively. The low end is warm and round rather than aggressive. Tracks breathe through careful use of silence and dynamic builds. The goal is a hypnotic, dance-floor-ready sound that rewards both active listening and ambient enjoyment. Production quality ranges from polished studio tracks to raw, spontaneous creations.

sub.d: A polished, vocal-forward style with R&B influences, smooth melodies, and refined production. Focuses on catchy hooks and radio-friendly arrangements while maintaining the core Amapiano groove.
Raw, bass-heavy Amapiano with stripped-back production and emphasis on deep grooves. Less polished than mainstream Amapiano, it stays close to the genre's township roots with gritty textures.

A bridge between kwaito and Amapiano, featuring call-and-response vocals, township slang, and heavier kick patterns. Represents the genre's direct lineage from 90s South African dance music.

dna: Born in the mid-2000s as a tribute to 1980s electronic culture. Driven by a steady 4/4 kick at 80–118 BPM with gated reverb snares and punchy LinnDrum patterns.

Analog synths (Juno-106, DX7), drum machines (LinnDrum, TR-808), gated reverb snare, electric guitar leads, bass synth, and vocoder.
Minor-key progressions dominate — i–VI–III–VII is the classic move. Lush detuned pads, arpeggiated sequences, and dramatic key changes.

dna: Indie pop emerged in the early 1980s UK as a DIY alternative to mainstream pop, rooted in post-punk's independence ethos but with a melodic, accessible twist. Labels like Creation, Sarah Records, and C86 compilations defined the early sound. By the 2000s, bands like The Postal Service, Vampire Weekend, and MGMT had brought indie pop to mainstream success, while the 2010s saw artists like Clairo, Rex Orange County, and boy pablo popularize bedroom indie pop.

Indie pop follows traditional pop songwriting — verse-chorus-verse — but with creative deviations. Songs emphasize melody above all, with catchy hooks delivered through guitars, synths, or vocals. Bridges often introduce unexpected chord changes or stripped-back moments. Arrangements tend to be cleaner and more spacious than indie rock, allowing each element room to breathe.

Jangly electric and acoustic guitars are central, often using chorus or reverb effects. Synthesizers range from warm analog pads to sparkly digital arpeggios. Drums are typically understated — programmed beats, brushed kit, or simple patterns with hand claps and tambourine. Bass stays melodic and supportive. Glockenspiel, ukulele, and whistling appear as textural accents.

Indie pop production values charm over perfection. The aesthetic ranges from lo-fi bedroom recordings to polished studio productions, but always retains a sense of intimacy and personality. Reverb and delay create dreamy atmospheres. The mix is typically bright and mid-focused, with vocals sitting clearly in front. The goal is music that feels personal and handcrafted, even at its most radio-friendly.

Guitar-driven indie pop with bright, chiming Rickenbacker-style arpeggios and upbeat rhythms. R.E.M., The Smiths, and Real Estate exemplify the ringing guitar sound and melodic focus.
A blend of folk's acoustic warmth with pop's catchiness and indie's creative independence. Fleet Foxes, Bon Iver, and Phoebe Bridgers merge organic textures with contemporary pop sensibility.
Atmospheric indie pop drenched in reverb, delay, and ethereal vocals. Cocteau Twins, Beach House, and Alvvays create immersive soundscapes that blur the line between pop melody and ambient texture.

dna: Brian Eno coined the term with Ambient 1: Music for Airports in 1978, defining music that could be "as ignorable as it is interesting." Roots trace to Erik Satie's furniture music, Tangerine Dream's cosmic explorations, and early tape-loop experiments. Ambient rejects traditional rhythm and melody in favor of atmosphere, texture, and deep listening.

Ambient abandons conventional song structure entirely. Pieces evolve through gradual textural shifts, long-form arcs spanning five to thirty-plus minutes, and slow timbral transformations. There are no verses, no choruses — instead, layers fade in and out, creating a sense of continuous, organic movement without clearly defined sections.

Synthesizers (analog and digital) form the harmonic foundation. Granular processors and spectral tools create evolving textures from any sound source. Field recordings — rain, wind, ocean, forest — ground the music in the physical world. Extensive reverb and delay processing turn brief sounds into vast spatial environments. Some artists incorporate piano, guitar, or voice processed beyond recognition.

Sustained drones on a single root note or fifth provide a stable harmonic floor. Modal clusters — groups of notes from a single scale played simultaneously — create floating, non-functional harmony. Harmonic movement is minimal and glacial. Dissonance is used sparingly and always resolves into consonance. The focus is on timbre and spatial depth rather than chord progression.

sub.d: Ominous drones, industrial textures, and unsettling atmospheres. Lustmord, Atrium Carceri, and Bohren & der Club of Gore create sonic landscapes of dread and tension.
Extended sustained tones with minimal variation — La Monte Young's Theatre of Eternal Music, Stars of the Lid, and Earth explored the meditative power of pure sustained sound.
Cosmic synthesizer journeys evoking the vastness of outer space. Tangerine Dream, Klaus Schulze, and Steve Roach paint interstellar soundscapes with sweeping pads and sequencers.
Subtle rhythmic pulses beneath ambient textures — The Orb, Aphex Twin's Selected Ambient Works, and Biosphere blended electronic beats with deep atmospheric layers.
Soothing, intentionally calming music for relaxation and meditation. Enya, Kitaro, and Deuter use acoustic instruments and soft synths to promote wellness and tranquility.
Warm pads and gentle four-on-the-floor rhythms creating a dreamlike dance-floor experience. The KLF's Chill Out and The Orb's Adventures Beyond the Ultraworld defined the style.

dna: J-Pop evolved from 1960s–70s kayokyoku (Japanese popular song) influenced by Western rock, folk, and Motown. The term emerged in the early 1990s during a commercial boom led by artists like Hikaru Utada, Mr. Children, and B'z. Anime theme songs became a massive driver, while the rise of Vocaloid and internet culture in the 2000s created new creative pathways. Today, artists like Kenshi Yonezu and YOASOBI bridge traditional J-Pop craft with digital-native production.

J-Pop favors complex A-B-C song structures that go beyond standard verse-chorus patterns. Dramatic key changes — often modulating up a half or whole step — build emotional intensity. Songs frequently include distinct melodic sections that don't repeat, giving each part its own identity. Anime tie-in songs often feature extended instrumental intros and outros.

A wide palette spanning electric and acoustic guitars, synthesizers, piano, orchestral strings, and programmed drums. City pop leans on slap bass, electric piano, and lush synth pads. Visual kei uses distorted guitars and heavy drums. Idol pop layers bright synths with handclap rhythms. Acoustic arrangements with piano and strings dominate ballad territory.

J-Pop is renowned for its harmonic sophistication. Complex chord progressions featuring secondary dominants, borrowed chords from parallel keys, diminished passing chords, and chromatic bass lines are standard. The influence of composers like Ryuichi Sakamoto and Tatsuro Yamashita runs deep. Melodies tend toward wide intervallic leaps and intricate rhythmic phrasing, creating an emotional expressiveness that distinguishes J-Pop from its Western counterparts.

sub.d: Groovy, funk-influenced Japanese pop with jazz harmony, slap bass, and warm analog synths. Pioneered by Tatsuro Yamashita and Mariya Takeuchi, now enjoying a massive global revival through internet curation.

Theme songs and scores for anime spanning every genre — from epic orchestral battle themes to tender piano ballads. Artists like LiSA, Aimer, and YOASOBI dominate this space with emotionally charged performances.
Theatrical Japanese rock with elaborate costumes, dramatic arrangements, and genre-blending from metal to gothic to symphonic. X Japan, Dir En Grey, and the GazettE define the movement's intensity.

dna: Drill emerged in Chicago's South Side around 2010-2012, pioneered by artists like Chief Keef, Lil Durk, and King Louie. The sound crossed the Atlantic to London, where producers like 808Melo and artists like Headie One transformed it into UK drill with faster tempos and distinct rhythmic patterns. By 2020, Brooklyn drill — led by Pop Smoke and Sheff G — fused both schools into a new dominant sound.

Drill tracks are loop-based with minimal harmonic movement. A typical structure features a short melodic intro, alternating verse sections with ad-libs and vocal effects, and occasional beat switches or breakdowns. Unlike traditional song forms, drill prioritizes rhythmic intensity and flow over chorus hooks — though melodic drill has increasingly adopted catchy refrains.

The 808 bass — pitched, distorted, and sliding between notes — is drill's backbone. Hi-hats are programmed with complex rolls and velocity variations. Dark melodic elements come from detuned pianos, minor-key string patches, plucked synths, and eerie pads. Snares and claps are layered for maximum punch, often with aggressive compression.

Drill production is deliberately sparse and menacing. Space in the mix is as important as the sounds themselves. Producers use heavy sidechain compression on the 808, precise hi-hat programming with triplet and roll patterns, and dark atmospheric textures to create tension. The goal is visceral impact — every element serves the rhythm and energy of the track.

sub.d: The original drill sound — slow, heavy 808s, trap-influenced hi-hats, and raw vocal delivery. Chief Keef, Lil Durk, and G Herbo defined this aggressive, street-rooted style.
London's adaptation features faster BPMs, complex sliding 808 patterns, and a bouncier rhythm. Headie One, Central Cee, and Digga D lead the scene with sharp wordplay over dark production.

New York's drill wave fuses UK drill's tempo with American vocal styles and sample-heavy production. Pop Smoke, Fivio Foreign, and Kay Flock popularized the Woo-era sound with aggressive energy and iconic ad-libs.
A softer take on drill combining dark production with melodic hooks and autotune vocals. Artists like Central Cee and Lil Tjay blend drill's rhythmic intensity with pop-accessible melodies.
A fusion of drill's 808 patterns with Afrobeats rhythms and melodies. Emerging from London and Lagos, it blends West African musical sensibility with drill's aggressive production framework.
A fusion of pluggnb's dreamy, lush production with drill's rhythmic intensity. Features ethereal melodies over aggressive drum patterns, creating a hypnotic contrast.
